data.title: The Thaw in the Loft
data.rumour: With the thaw, there are cobwebs on the Saint Brine's bell rope again.
data.teaser: The thaw. Meltwater drips from every gutter on Main Street, and this morning there's a single fine thread of silk across the shop door, glittering, the first since October.
about: A March epilogue to The Cabinet of Curiosities, for runs where the spider queen went to Providence or was cleared out of Saint Brine's loft. With the thaw, Father Ignatius says the egg sacs under the attic boards are moving, and will hatch on the first warm night (§{broodIgnatius}).

On that night (§{broodNight}) hundreds of tiny spiderlings climb up to balloon away. Open the louvers under the bell and let the wind carry them out over the marsh (Silk on the Wind), let Sal gas them with sulphur candles (Sulphur Again), or text Coralie Vance, the Providence collector, who'll take them all for $200 (Shipped to Providence, Again).

broodIgnatius.title: Father Ignatius: the egg sacs are moving

text: The thaw has come through the roof of the loft, the way it always does. And under the attic boards, where she was, the egg sacs have started to move.

text.then: Dr. Ladd says it's the spring. He says the empty drawer was a cocoon, and the queen came out of it, and the sacs are the rest of her. He says they'll hatch with the first warm night, and he says it as if it's good news.
text.else: She went to Providence in October. Her eggs didn't. Sal says they'll hatch with the first warm night. Sal says it with his hand on a box of sulphur candles.

text: Come up with us. {placed:brood-night} night. The forecast says it will be warm.

narrate: Saint Brine's loft on the first warm night of the year. Meltwater ticks off the slates. Under the attic boards the old silk is grey and sagging, and the egg sacs on the posts are splitting, one after another, like seed pods.
They come out pale as frost, hundreds of them, each the size of a fingernail, and climb to the highest thing they can find, and stand on tiptoe with their back ends in the air.

then.narrate: Dr. Ladd has brought her, in her drawer, under new glass. He sets the drawer on the boards and slides the glass back. She doesn't come out. She lifts two front legs toward the brood, slow as a priest blessing a congregation.

then.text: They're going to balloon. Spin a thread and let the wind take them. It's what the small ones do. They can go a hundred miles. Isn't that wonderful?

else.text: Four hundred of them, easy. Each one's going to be the size of a dinner plate by August. I've got the candles. Say the word.

else.narrate: Your phone buzzes. A text from a Providence number: "I hear it's warm in Hollow Neck tonight. I have a van and a great many jars. C.V."

choose.label: Open the louvers under the bell and let the wind take them

narrate: You and Father Ignatius haul the louvers open under the bell. The warm air comes in off the marsh. All at once, as if somebody gave a signal, four hundred threads go up into the dark, catch the light from the street, and lift.
They go out of Saint Brine's tower like smoke, a long glittering ribbon of silk, over the Green and the boatyard and out across Hob's Marsh in the moonlight, and are gone.

then.text: In the morning there will be silk on every reed from here to Gull Point. The children will think it's frost.

choose.label: Let Sal light the sulphur candles

then.narrate: Sal comes up the ladder with his box of candles. Dr. Ladd closes the glass over the queen without a word and carries her down past him.
Yellow smoke and the smell of a thousand struck matches. The small ones fall off their tiptoes like snow. It takes nine minutes. Nobody says anything for all nine.

then.why: Gassed the brood in Saint Brine's loft
Gassed the brood in Saint Brine's loft

then.narrate: Coralie Vance's van is outside Saint Brine's in forty minutes, as if it was already on the road. She comes up the ladder in a good coat with a sable brush and a crate of jam jars, and collects them, one at a time, talking to each one.

then.text: She isn't a scientist, is she.

then.narrate: Two hundred dollars in a cream envelope on your counter in the morning, and a card: "For the drawer. They always come home in the end. C.V."

then.why: Coralie Vance paid for the brood

epilogue.line: Every reed on Hob's Marsh was silver with silk on the first morning of spring. The children called it frost. A birdwatcher from Duxbury wrote to the Gazette about it, three pages, very excited.
Saint Brine's loft smells of struck matches again. The bell rope is clean. Father Ignatius rings it a little harder than he needs to.
A natural history museum in Providence has reopened its wing, with a new display of four hundred jars, labelled in fountain pen: HOLLOW NECK, MARCH.

rumour: The thaw got into Saint Brine's loft. I sold Father Ignatius another tarp, and he asked me if I had anything for, quote, a great many small spiders.
I said I had a broom. He said that wasn't what he meant. I didn't ask what he meant.

react.wind: There was silk on every reed on the marsh this morning. Like frost. My grandson put some in a jar. I made him let it go. I don't know why. It felt right.
react.gassed: Sal bought out my whole shelf of sulphur candles. Said it was for the church. Said the Lord didn't mind. I'd mind, if I were a spider.
react.vance: A woman with a van full of jam jars bought every jar I had. Sixty jars. Paid cash. Asked for lids with holes in.
